decks.title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants — Part 1: Site, pigments and the light reaction
goals: Describe the chloroplast and the pigments involved in photosynthesis
Explain the light reaction: photosystems, electron transport, cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
Explain the chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis

slides.heading: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — where light energy is captured and how it becomes ATP and NADPH.

nodes.label: Light reaction: ATP, NADPH and oxygen
Calvin cycle: sugar from carbon dioxide

visual.alt: Flow from light energy through the light reaction to the Calvin cycle

slides.narration: Almost all life depends on photosynthesis. Green plants use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and release oxygen. The process has two linked parts. The light reaction captures energy as ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle uses them to make sugar. In this part we study the first.

slides.heading: The site: the chloroplast
slides.body_md: In green plants photosynthesis takes place mainly in the **leaves**, in **chloroplasts**. The chloroplast has a **double membrane**. **Grana** (stacks of **thylakoids**) joined by **stroma lamellae** lie in the **stroma**.

slides.narration: The light reaction needs pigments and takes place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana. The stroma contains the enzymes that fix carbon dioxide, so the Calvin cycle happens there. The membranes of the stroma lamellae lack photosystem two and the enzyme that makes NADPH.

slides.heading: Photosynthetic pigments
slides.body_md: **Chlorophyll a** is the chief pigment. **Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids** are **accessory pigments**: they absorb light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a, widen the range of light used, and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

rows: Chief pigment; forms the reaction centre

visual.alt: Table of the four leaf pigments with their colours and roles

slides.narration: Leaf pigments can be separated by paper chromatography. Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment that traps light. The other three are accessory pigments. They absorb light at other wavelengths and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a, and they also protect it from damage by too much light.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a pigment chromatogram
slides.body_md: A leaf extract is run on paper with the solvent front 12 cm from the origin. The four bands lie 11.4 cm (carotenoids), 9 cm (xanthophylls), 6 cm (chlorophyll a), 4.2 cm (chlorophyll b) from the origin. Find each Rf value and say which pigment is most soluble in the solvent.
bullets: $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by pigment}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$, so carotenoids: $\dfrac{11.4}{12} = 0.95$.
Xanthophylls: $\dfrac{9}{12} = 0.75$; chlorophyll a: $\dfrac{6}{12} = 0.5$; chlorophyll b: $\dfrac{4.2}{12} = 0.35$.
Carotenoids travel farthest, so they are the most soluble in this solvent.

slides.narration: The retention factor is the distance moved by the pigment divided by the distance moved by the solvent. Carotenoids moved eleven point four centimetres out of twelve, which gives zero point nine five, the highest value. Chlorophyll b moved the least, so it has the lowest value and is least soluble in this solvent.

slides.heading: Absorption and action spectra
slides.body_md: Chlorophyll a absorbs mainly in the **violet-blue and red** regions. The **action spectrum** of photosynthesis follows the **absorption** of the pigments together, so green light is the least effective.

visual.alt: Absorption spectra of chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids with the action spectrum of photosynthesis

slides.narration: The absorption spectrum shows how much light a pigment takes in at each wavelength. Chlorophyll a absorbs strongly in the violet blue and the red. The action spectrum, which shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength, closely matches the combined absorption of all the pigments. Little green light is absorbed, which is why leaves look green.

slides.heading: Photosystems and reaction centres
slides.body_md: The pigments are organised into **light-harvesting complexes** within **photosystem I (PS I)** and **photosystem II (PS II)**. Hundreds of pigment molecules act as an **antenna**; one chlorophyll a molecule forms the **reaction centre**.

rows: Grana thylakoids; not in stroma lamellae

visual.alt: Table of photosystem II and photosystem I with their reaction centres and absorption peaks

slides.narration: Each photosystem has an antenna of many pigment molecules that funnels light energy to a single chlorophyll a molecule, the reaction centre. In photosystem one the reaction centre absorbs best at seven hundred nanometres, and in photosystem two at six hundred and eighty nanometres.

slides.heading: The thylakoid membrane at work
slides.body_md: The light reaction takes place on the **thylakoid membrane**: water is split on the **lumen** side, electrons flow along the carriers, **NADP reductase** works on the **stroma** side, and **ATP synthase** makes ATP.

slides.narration: Light excites photosystem two, and water is split on the lumen side, releasing oxygen, protons and electrons. The electrons pass along carriers to photosystem one. There, light excites them again and they reach NADP reductase on the stroma side, which makes NADPH. Protons build up in the lumen and flow out through ATP synthase.

slides.heading: The Z scheme: non-cyclic electron flow
slides.body_md: In **non-cyclic photophosphorylation** both photosystems work in series: electrons move from **water → PS II → plastoquinone → cytochrome b₆f → plastocyanin → PS I → ferredoxin → NADP⁺**. The result is **ATP, NADPH and oxygen**.

slides.narration: The path of the electron looks like the letter Z when drawn against energy. Light raises the electron in photosystem two, it runs downhill to photosystem one, and light lifts it again. Finally it reaches NADP plus, which is reduced to NADPH. Water splitting replaces the electrons lost by photosystem two, and releases oxygen.

slides.heading: Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
slides.body_md: Compare the two routes by **which photosystems act** and **what they produce**.

rows: Water to NADP⁺; electrons do not return
Stroma lamellae; when light above 680 nm only

visual.alt: Table comparing non-cyclic and cyclic photophosphorylation

slides.narration: In cyclic photophosphorylation only photosystem one works. The excited electron passes down a chain of carriers and returns to photosystem one, so only ATP is made, no NADPH and no oxygen. It takes place in the stroma lamellae, and when only light of wavelengths longer than six hundred and eighty nanometres is available.

slides.heading: The chemiosmotic hypothesis
slides.body_md: ATP is made because of a **proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane**, with **protons accumulating in the lumen**.

nodes.label: Water split in the lumen: H⁺ released
Carriers move H⁺ from stroma to lumen
NADP reductase uses H⁺ in the stroma
Gradient: more H⁺ in the lumen
ATP synthase: CF₀ channel and CF₁ make ATP

visual.alt: Flow from three proton-moving events to a proton gradient and then ATP synthase

slides.narration: Three events raise the proton concentration in the lumen. Water is split inside it. Carriers move protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons pass. And NADP reductase uses up protons on the stroma side. The breakdown of this gradient through the channel of ATP synthase changes the shape of its knob and makes ATP.

slides.heading: Quick check: the proton gradient
slides.body_md: Choose where protons are stored.
slides.narration: Quick check. On which side of the thylakoid membrane do protons accumulate?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from water to NADPH
slides.body_md: The overall equation for one glucose needs 12 water molecules to be split. How many oxygen molecules and electrons result, and how many NADPH can those electrons reduce? (Each NADPH takes 2 electrons.)
bullets: Each $2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives one $\text{O}_2$ and $4$ electrons, so 12 water molecules give $\dfrac{12}{2} = 6$ oxygen molecules.
Electrons: $12 \times 2 = 24$.
NADPH: $\dfrac{24}{2} = 12$, exactly the number of NADPH the Calvin cycle needs for one glucose.

visual.alt: Worked table: 12 water, 6 oxygen, 24 electrons, 12 NADPH

slides.narration: Splitting two water molecules gives one oxygen molecule and four electrons. Twelve waters give six oxygen molecules and twenty four electrons. Each NADPH takes two electrons, so twenty four electrons make twelve NADPH, exactly the amount the Calvin cycle needs for one glucose. The oxygen comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Chloroplast: grana (light reaction) and stroma (Calvin cycle).
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment; chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory.
PS II (P680) and PS I (P700); the Z scheme gives ATP, NADPH and O₂.
Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only. Non-cyclic: both, ATP + NADPH + O₂.
Chemiosmosis: H⁺ gradient in the lumen drives ATP synthase.

visual.alt: Flow from carbon dioxide fixation through reduction to sugar and RuBP regeneration

slides.narration: The light reaction makes ATP and NADPH, but sugar is made in the stroma by the Calvin cycle. In this part we count what the cycle costs, see how C four plants change the story, understand why photorespiration wastes energy, and ask what limits the rate of photosynthesis.

slides.heading: The Calvin cycle
slides.body_md: The Calvin cycle occurs in the **stroma** of all photosynthetic plants. It has three stages: **carboxylation, reduction and regeneration**.

slides.narration: Carbon dioxide combines with the five carbon sugar RuBP, in a reaction catalysed by RuBisCO, to form two molecules of the three carbon acid PGA. PGA is reduced to a three carbon sugar using ATP and NADPH. Most of this sugar is used to regenerate RuBP, which also needs ATP. After three turns, one three carbon sugar is the net gain.

slides.heading: The three stages in detail
slides.body_md: Learn each stage by its **input, enzyme or energy source, and output**.

rows: RuBP + CO₂ → 2 PGA, catalysed by **RuBisCO**, the most abundant enzyme on Earth
PGA → triose phosphate (G3P) in two steps: phosphorylation, then reduction
RuBP is regenerated so the cycle can continue

visual.alt: Table of carboxylation, reduction and regeneration in the Calvin cycle

slides.narration: The first stable product, PGA, has three carbons, so plants using only this pathway are called C three plants. Reduction needs two ATP and two NADPH for every carbon dioxide fixed. Regeneration of RuBP needs one more ATP. So each carbon dioxide costs three ATP and two NADPH.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the cost of one glucose
slides.body_md: How many turns of the Calvin cycle, how many ATP and how many NADPH are needed to make one glucose (6 carbons)? Per CO₂ the cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
bullets: One CO$_2$ is fixed per turn, so glucose needs $6$ turns.
ATP: $6 \times 3 = 18$.
NADPH: $6 \times 2 = 12$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 6 turns, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH

slides.narration: Each turn fixes one carbon dioxide, so a six carbon glucose needs six turns. At three ATP per turn that is eighteen ATP, and at two NADPH per turn it is twelve NADPH. These totals match the textbook figures for the C three pathway.

slides.narration: The primary acceptor of carbon dioxide in the mesophyll cell is PEP, a three carbon molecule, and the enzyme is PEP carboxylase. The four carbon acid moves into the bundle sheath cell, where it is broken down to release carbon dioxide. The three carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll and is turned back into PEP.

slides.heading: Kranz anatomy and C3 versus C4
slides.body_md: **Kranz anatomy:** large **bundle sheath** cells around the vascular bundles, with **thick walls impervious to gases** and no intercellular spaces. **RuBisCO is only in the bundle sheath**; the Calvin cycle runs there.

rows: PEP in mesophyll; RuBP in bundle sheath

visual.alt: Table comparing C3 and C4 plants

slides.narration: C four plants have a special leaf anatomy called Kranz anatomy. Large bundle sheath cells surround the veins, with thick walls and no air spaces. Because the carbon dioxide is concentrated there, C four plants have no photorespiration, tolerate higher temperatures and have greater productivity.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: C3 versus C4 energy cost
slides.body_md: A C4 plant spends 2 extra ATP per CO₂ to regenerate PEP, so it needs 5 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂. Compare the ATP needed for one glucose in C3 and C4 plants, and the ATP : NADPH ratios.
bullets: Extra ATP in C$_4$: $30 - 18 = 12$, which is $6 \times 2$.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing ATP and NADPH needs of C3 and C4 plants

slides.narration: A C three plant needs eighteen ATP for one glucose, a C four plant thirty, because of two extra ATP for each carbon dioxide. The NADPH need is the same, twelve. So C four plants need more ATP in proportion to NADPH, which cyclic flow of electrons can help to supply. The extra cost pays off in hot, bright places.

slides.heading: Photorespiration
slides.body_md: RuBisCO can bind **O₂ as well as CO₂**. In a high O₂ and low CO₂ situation, **RuBP + O₂ → PGA + phosphoglycolate**. There is **no sugar, ATP or NADPH made**, and CO₂ is released: it is a **wasteful** process.

visual.alt: Flow comparing carboxylation with the oxygenase reaction of RuBisCO that starts photorespiration

slides.narration: The enzyme RuBisCO has an active site that binds both carbon dioxide and oxygen. When oxygen is high and carbon dioxide low, RuBP takes up oxygen and one of the products is phosphoglycolate. No sugar, ATP or NADPH is made, and the pathway through three organelles releases carbon dioxide, so it wastes energy. C four plants avoid it by concentrating carbon dioxide at RuBisCO.

slides.heading: Factors affecting photosynthesis
slides.body_md: The rate depends on **light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water**, and on internal factors such as the number, age and orientation of leaves and the amount of chlorophyll.

rows: Rate rises with intensity, then saturates; about 10 percent of full sunlight is enough for saturation
Present at about 0.03–0.04 percent; raising it increases the rate. C4 plants saturate near 360 µL per L; C3 plants respond up to about 450 µL per L
Dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature sensitive; C4 plants have a higher optimum than C3 plants
Water stress closes stomata, cutting CO₂ supply, and wilting reduces leaf area

visual.alt: Table of external factors affecting photosynthesis

slides.narration: The usual amount of carbon dioxide in air is limiting for C three plants, so greenhouse crops such as tomato and bell pepper give higher yields when the air is enriched with it. Temperature affects the enzyme controlled reactions, and water stress closes stomata and so cuts off the supply of carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Blackman’s law of limiting factors
slides.body_md: **Law of limiting factors:** if a process depends on several factors, its rate is determined by the factor **nearest its minimum value**. At low light, light limits; once light is enough, **CO₂ or temperature** takes over.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which factor is limiting?
slides.body_md: Use the graph model (arbitrary units): rate with light at 4 percent, CO₂ at 300 µL per L and 25 °C is 18. Predict what happens to the rate when (i) light is raised to 10 percent, and (ii) CO₂ is then raised to 450 µL per L.
bullets: (i) Light at 4 percent is limiting (18). At 10 percent the rate rises to only 30, because now **CO₂ is limiting**.
(ii) Raising CO₂ to 450 lifts the rate to 45, because the added CO₂ removes the limit.
(iii) A further rise in light to 20 percent leaves it at 45, because **CO₂, not light, is limiting** again.

slides.narration: At low light, more light raises the rate, so light is limiting. At ten percent light the rate stops rising with light, and carbon dioxide has become limiting. Adding carbon dioxide lifts the rate. After that, extra light brings no further increase, because carbon dioxide is limiting again.

bullets: Calvin cycle in the stroma: carboxylation (RuBisCO), reduction, regeneration; 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂; 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
C4: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll, Calvin cycle in bundle sheath; 5 ATP per CO₂; no photorespiration.

Factors: light, CO₂, temperature, water.
Blackman: the factor nearest its minimum sets the rate.

sections.heading: 1. Site and pigments of photosynthesis
sections.body_md:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use **light energy** to make **carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water**, releasing **oxygen**. In green plants it takes place mainly in the **leaves**, in the **chloroplasts**. A chloroplast has a **double membrane** enclosing the **stroma**; in the stroma lie the **grana**, stacks of flattened sacs called **thylakoids**, joined by **stroma lamellae**. The **light reaction** takes place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana; the stroma holds the enzymes of the **Calvin cycle**. The membranes of the stroma lamellae lack photosystem II and NADP reductase.

Four kinds of pigment are found in the leaf and can be separated by **paper chromatography**: **chlorophyll a** (bright or blue green), **chlorophyll b** (yellow green), **xanthophylls** (yellow) and **carotenoids** (yellow to yellow-orange). On the paper the carotenoids travel farthest and chlorophyll b least. **Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment**; the others are **accessory pigments** that absorb light at other wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll a, so enabling a wider range of wavelengths to be used, and that also **protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation**. In chromatography the retention factor is $R_f$ = distance moved by the pigment divided by distance moved by the solvent front.

Chlorophyll a absorbs mostly in the **violet-blue and red** regions of the spectrum. The **absorption spectrum** shows the light absorbed at each wavelength; the **action spectrum** shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength, and it closely follows the absorption of the pigments together. Green light is the least effective.

(The Rf values and band positions in the figures are illustrative; the order of bands depends on the solvent used, and the textbook order is quoted.)

sections.heading: 2. Light reaction: cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
sections.body_md:
The pigments are organised into **light-harvesting complexes (LHC)** within **photosystem I (PS I)** and **photosystem II (PS II)**. Each photosystem has an **antenna** of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins; all of them except one chlorophyll a molecule pass the energy to this single molecule, the **reaction centre**. The reaction centre of **PS I is P700** (absorption peak 700 nm) and of **PS II is P680** (680 nm).

**Non-cyclic photophosphorylation (the Z scheme).** In **PS II** the reaction-centre chlorophyll absorbs 680 nm red light; electrons are excited and transferred to an electron acceptor and then **downhill** through **plastoquinone**, the **cytochrome b₆f complex** and **plastocyanin** to **PS I**. The electrons lost from PS II are replaced by **splitting of water** (on the lumen side, associated with PS II): $2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\,\text{H}^+ + \text{O}_2 + 4\,e^-$. This is the source of the **oxygen** released. In **PS I** the electrons are excited again, passed to an acceptor of greater redox potential and move downhill through **ferredoxin** to **NADP reductase** (on the stroma side), which reduces **NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺**. The result is **ATP, NADPH and oxygen**, and the electrons do not return to PS II.

**Cyclic photophosphorylation.** Only **PS I** acts: the excited electron passes to an acceptor, then down a chain through the **cytochrome b₆f complex** and **plastocyanin** and returns to PS I. Because PS II is not involved, there is **no water splitting, no oxygen and no NADPH**; only **ATP** is made. It occurs in the **stroma lamellae**, when only light of wavelengths longer than 680 nm is available.

**Chemiosmotic hypothesis.** ATP synthesis is linked to the **proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane**, with **protons accumulating in the lumen**. Three events raise the proton concentration in the lumen: (i) **splitting of water** inside the lumen releases protons; (ii) as electrons move through the photosystems, the carrier **plastoquinone** removes protons from the **stroma** and releases them in the lumen; (iii) **NADP reductase** uses protons from the **stroma** to reduce NADP⁺, further lowering the proton concentration in the stroma. ATP synthase has a transmembrane channel, **CF₀**, and a knob, **CF₁**, on the stroma side. Breakdown of the gradient as protons flow out through CF₀ causes a conformational change in CF₁ that makes **ATP**.

**Count.** The overall equation for one glucose is 6 CO₂ + 12 H₂O → glucose + 6 O₂ + 6 H₂O, so 12 water molecules are split: that gives 6 O₂ and 24 electrons, enough for 12 NADPH, as the Calvin cycle needs.

sections.heading: 3. Calvin cycle, C4 pathway and photorespiration
sections.body_md:
**Calvin cycle (C₃ pathway).** The cycle takes place in the **stroma** of all photosynthetic plants. Melvin Calvin found, using radioactive carbon, that the first stable product of CO₂ fixation is a **3-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA)**. It has three stages. **Carboxylation:** CO₂ combines with the 5-carbon **ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)**, catalysed by **RuBisCO** (the most abundant enzyme on Earth), giving two molecules of PGA. **Reduction:** PGA is phosphorylated and reduced to **triose phosphate (G3P)**, using **2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂**. **Regeneration:** RuBP is regenerated, which needs **1 ATP**. So for every CO₂ fixed the cycle uses **3 ATP and 2 NADPH**, and **six turns** (six CO₂) are needed to make one glucose: **18 ATP and 12 NADPH**. In three turns, 3 RuBP (15 C) and 3 CO₂ give 6 PGA (18 C), then 6 G3P; five G3P regenerate 3 RuBP and one G3P is the net gain.

**C₄ pathway.** Plants adapted to dry tropical regions (such as maize and sugarcane) have the C₄ pathway. They have **Kranz anatomy**: large **bundle sheath cells** around the vascular bundles with **thick walls impervious to gases** and no intercellular spaces. The primary acceptor of CO₂ is **phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP, 3-carbon)** in the **mesophyll cells**; the enzyme is **PEP carboxylase (PEPcase)** and the first product is the 4-carbon **oxaloacetic acid (OAA)**, converted to **malic or aspartic acid**. These C₄ acids move to the **bundle sheath cells**, where they are broken down to release **CO₂** and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle** (RuBisCO is present only in the bundle sheath), and the 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll to regenerate PEP, which costs 2 ATP. C₄ plants therefore need **5 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂** (30 ATP per glucose). They **tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light, lack photorespiration and have greater biomass productivity**.

**Photorespiration.** The active site of **RuBisCO** can bind **CO₂ or O₂** depending on their relative concentrations. In a high O₂, low CO₂ situation, RuBP binds O₂ and forms **one PGA and one phosphoglycolate (a 2-carbon molecule)** instead of two PGA. In this pathway, which involves the **chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion**, **no sugar and no ATP or NADPH is made; CO₂ is released and energy is used**, so it is a **wasteful** process. It occurs in **C₃ plants**; **C₄ plants avoid it** because CO₂ is concentrated at RuBisCO in the bundle sheath, and PEP carboxylase has no affinity for O₂. The biological function of photorespiration is not clearly known.

sections.heading: 4. Factors affecting photosynthesis
sections.body_md:
The rate of photosynthesis is affected by **internal factors** (number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ concentration, and the amount of chlorophyll) and by **external factors**: light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water.

**Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905):** if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor that is **nearest to its minimal value**; it is the factor that directly affects the process if its quantity is changed.

**Light.** At low light intensity the rate of photosynthesis rises with it; at higher intensities the rate does not increase further because other factors become limiting. Light saturation occurs at about **10 percent of full sunlight**, except in plants of shade; light quality and duration also matter. **Carbon dioxide** is the major limiting factor: its concentration in the atmosphere is very low (**0.03 to 0.04 percent**), and increasing it up to about 0.05 percent raises the rate. At high light, both C₃ and C₄ plants respond, but **C₄ plants saturate at about 360 µL per L** whereas **C₃ plants respond to increases up to about 450 µL per L**, so present CO₂ levels limit C₃ plants; **tomato and bell pepper** grown in CO₂-enriched greenhouses give higher yields. **Temperature.** The dark (Calvin cycle) reactions are enzymatic and temperature controlled; the light reactions are less sensitive. **C₄ plants have a higher temperature optimum** than C₃ plants, and the optimum relates to the plant's habitat (tropical plants have a higher optimum than temperate plants). **Water.** Its effect is largely through the plant: **water stress closes stomata, reducing CO₂ availability**, and wilting reduces leaf area and metabolic activity.

(The rates in the graph are in arbitrary units from a simple minimum-of-factors model that illustrates the law; real curves are smoother.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide (it comes from the splitting of water).
- Saying cyclic photophosphorylation makes NADPH or oxygen (it makes only ATP and involves only PS I).
- Reversing the sides of the thylakoid: protons accumulate in the **lumen**; NADP reductase and ATP synthase's knob are on the **stroma** side.
- Writing the Calvin cycle needs 2 ATP per CO₂ (it is 3 ATP: 2 for reduction and 1 for regeneration) or forgetting that glucose needs **6 turns**.
- Saying C₄ plants have no Calvin cycle (they fix CO₂ twice: PEP carboxylase first, then RuBisCO in the bundle sheath).
- Describing photorespiration as useful: no sugar, ATP or NADPH is formed.
- Naming the wrong limiting factor from a graph: the plateau shows that something other than the plotted variable is limiting.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a pigment colour, P680 or P700, the enzyme (RuBisCO, PEPcase), the first product (PGA or OAA), a site (stroma or lumen), Blackman's law.
- 2–3-mark answers: cyclic versus non-cyclic; chemiosmosis; the stages of the Calvin cycle; C₃ versus C₄; photorespiration; the factors affecting photosynthesis.
- 5-mark answers: light reaction with the Z scheme; Calvin cycle with energy count; C₄ pathway with Kranz anatomy.
- Numericals: Rf from a chromatogram; ATP and NADPH for n CO₂; turns for glucose; water, oxygen and electrons; reading limiting factors from rate data.

cards.front_md: Where in the cell does photosynthesis take place?
cards.back_md: In chloroplasts: light reaction on thylakoids of the grana, Calvin cycle in the stroma.

cards.front_md: Name the four leaf pigments and their colours.
cards.back_md: Chlorophyll a (bright or blue green), chlorophyll b (yellow green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange).

cards.front_md: Chief and accessory pigments?
cards.back_md: Chlorophyll a is chief; chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory.

cards.front_md: Why are accessory pigments useful?
cards.back_md: They widen the range of light used, pass energy to chlorophyll a, and protect it from photo-oxidation.

cards.front_md: Rf formula?
cards.back_md: Distance moved by the pigment divided by distance moved by the solvent front.

cards.front_md: Action spectrum versus absorption spectrum?
cards.back_md: Action: rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. Absorption: light absorbed. The action spectrum follows the combined absorption.

cards.front_md: Which parts of the spectrum does chlorophyll a absorb most?
cards.back_md: Violet-blue and red.

cards.front_md: Structure of a photosystem?
cards.back_md: Antenna of pigment molecules (light-harvesting complex) plus one chlorophyll a reaction centre.

cards.front_md: Reaction centres of PS I and PS II?
cards.back_md: PS I: P700. PS II: P680.

cards.front_md: Where does water splitting occur and what does it give?
cards.back_md: On the lumen side of PS II: 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + O₂ + 4 e⁻.

cards.front_md: Order of carriers in the Z scheme?
cards.back_md: PS II, plastoquinone, cytochrome b₆f, plastocyanin, PS I, ferredoxin, NADP reductase.

cards.front_md: Products of non-cyclic photophosphorylation?
cards.back_md: ATP, NADPH and oxygen.

cards.front_md: Cyclic photophosphorylation: photosystem, product, place?
cards.back_md: PS I only; ATP only; stroma lamellae.

cards.front_md: Which enzyme makes NADPH and on which side?
cards.back_md: NADP reductase, on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane.

cards.front_md: Three events that build the proton gradient?
cards.back_md: Water splitting in the lumen; plastoquinone moving H⁺ from stroma to lumen; NADP reductase using H⁺ from the stroma.

cards.front_md: Parts of ATP synthase?
cards.back_md: CF₀ channel in the membrane and CF₁ knob on the stroma side.

cards.front_md: First stable product of the Calvin cycle?
cards.back_md: 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA), a 3-carbon acid.

cards.front_md: Name the three stages of the Calvin cycle.
cards.back_md: Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration.

cards.front_md: Enzyme of carboxylation and the acceptor?
cards.back_md: RuBisCO; ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C).

cards.front_md: ATP and NADPH per CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
cards.back_md: 3 ATP (2 for reduction, 1 for regeneration) and 2 NADPH.

cards.front_md: ATP and NADPH for one glucose (C3)?
cards.back_md: 6 turns: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

cards.front_md: CO₂ acceptor and enzyme in mesophyll of C4 plants?
cards.back_md: PEP (3C); PEP carboxylase; first product oxaloacetate (4C).

cards.front_md: What is Kranz anatomy?
cards.back_md: Large, thick-walled bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles.

cards.front_md: ATP per CO₂ in C4 plants?
cards.back_md: 5 ATP (2 extra to regenerate PEP) and 2 NADPH.

cards.front_md: Features of C4 plants?
cards.back_md: Kranz anatomy; higher temperature optimum; respond to high light; no photorespiration; greater productivity.

cards.front_md: What is photorespiration?
cards.back_md: RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂: RuBP gives PGA and phosphoglycolate; no sugar, ATP or NADPH; CO₂ released; wasteful.

cards.front_md: State Blackman’s law of limiting factors.
cards.back_md: When several factors affect a process, its rate is set by the factor nearest its minimum value.

cards.front_md: Light saturation point?
cards.back_md: About 10 percent of full sunlight.

cards.front_md: Response of C3 and C4 plants to CO₂?
cards.back_md: C4 saturate near 360 µL per L; C3 respond up to about 450 µL per L.

cards.front_md: Effects of temperature and water?
cards.back_md: Dark reactions are temperature sensitive (C4 optimum higher); water stress closes stomata and cuts CO₂ supply.

questions.stem_md: A student runs a green leaf extract on chromatography paper. The band that lies lowest on the paper, nearest the origin, is yellow green. Which pigment forms this band?

options.text_md: Chlorophyll a
Chlorophyll b
Xanthophyll
Carotenoid

questions.solution_md: On the chromatogram the order from the top is carotenoids, xanthophylls, chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b; the yellow green band at the bottom is chlorophyll b — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student isolates a membrane fraction from chloroplasts that makes ATP in light but cannot split water or release oxygen, and it has no NADP reductase. It most probably came from

options.text_md: the grana thylakoids
stroma lamellae
the outer membrane
the stroma

questions.solution_md: The stroma lamellae lack photosystem II and NADP reductase, so they can only carry out cyclic photophosphorylation (ATP alone) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A mutant seedling that lacks carotenoids but has normal chlorophylls bleaches and dies in strong sunlight, although normal seedlings do well. Which role of carotenoids does this show?

options.text_md: They form the reaction centre of photosystem II.
They protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
They are the chief pigment that splits water.
They make NADPH from NADP⁺.

questions.solution_md: Accessory pigments, including carotenoids, protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation; the reaction centre is a chlorophyll a molecule — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A grower lights a seedling tray with a lamp that gives only green light and finds the seedlings grow very poorly. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: the leaf pigments absorb green light least, so little energy is trapped
green light is absorbed so strongly that the leaves overheat
green light destroys the thylakoid membranes
green light cannot reach the leaf surface

questions.solution_md: The absorption and action spectra both show that green light is the least effective for photosynthesis because it is absorbed least — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is not an accessory pigment of photosynthesis?

options.text_md: Chlorophyll a
Chlorophyll b
Xanthophyll
Carotenoid

questions.solution_md: Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment; chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An action spectrum of photosynthesis is a graph of

options.text_md: the light absorbed by chlorophyll a against the wavelength of light
the rate of photosynthesis against the temperature
the amount of oxygen released against the age of the leaf
the rate of photosynthesis against the wavelength of light

questions.solution_md: An action spectrum plots the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength; plotting absorption against wavelength gives the absorption spectrum — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The enzymes that fix carbon dioxide into sugar are located in the

options.text_md: lumen of the thylakoids
outer membrane of the chloroplast
stroma of the chloroplast
grana membranes

questions.solution_md: The Calvin cycle enzymes lie in the stroma, whereas the light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes of the grana — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the chromatogram of a leaf extract shown (bands A to D, ruler in centimetres, solvent front at 12 cm), the band of chlorophyll a is bright or blue green and lies at 6 cm. Which letter marks chlorophyll a?

options.text_md: A
B
D
C

questions.solution_md: Band D lies at 6 cm from the origin. Band C (11.4 cm) is carotenoids, A (9.0 cm) xanthophylls and B (4.2 cm) chlorophyll b — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish an absorption spectrum from an action spectrum, and say how the two compare for photosynthesis and what this shows.

answer.model_answer_md: An **absorption spectrum** shows how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength. An **action spectrum** shows the **rate of photosynthesis** at each wavelength. The action spectrum **closely follows the combined absorption spectra** of the pigments, with peaks in the violet-blue and red. This shows that the **light absorbed by the pigments drives photosynthesis**, and that green light is the least effective.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and state which stage of photosynthesis takes place in each part. Name the pigments present and the chief pigment.

answer.model_answer_md:
A **chloroplast** has a **double membrane**, the outer and inner membranes, enclosing the **stroma**. Inside the stroma are **grana**, stacks of flattened sacs called **thylakoids**, joined by **stroma lamellae**.

The **light reaction** takes place on the **thylakoid membranes** of the grana, where the pigments and photosystems lie. The membranes of the stroma lamellae lack photosystem II and NADP reductase. The **stroma** contains the enzymes of the **Calvin cycle**, where CO₂ is fixed into sugar.

The pigments are **chlorophyll a** (bright or blue green), **chlorophyll b** (yellow green), **xanthophylls** (yellow) and **carotenoids** (yellow to yellow-orange). **Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment**; the others are accessory pigments.

questions.stem_md: During a burst of light, 24 water molecules are split in a chloroplast. How many oxygen molecules are released?
questions.solution_md: Each $2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives one $\text{O}_2$, so $\dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ oxygen molecules.

questions.stem_md: The splitting of 24 water molecules releases 4 electrons for every 2 water molecules. If every electron goes to NADP⁺ and each NADPH takes 2 electrons, how many NADPH can be made?
questions.solution_md: Electrons $= 24 \times 2 = 48$, since each water gives 2; NADPH $= \dfrac{48}{2} = 24$.

questions.stem_md: Splitting two water molecules gives four protons. How many protons are released into the lumen by the splitting of 6 water molecules?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{6}{2} \times 4 = 12$ protons.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Non-cyclic** photophosphorylation uses **both photosystems** and the electrons pass from water to NADP⁺, giving **ATP, NADPH and oxygen**. **Cyclic** photophosphorylation uses **only photosystem I**; the electrons **return to PS I** and only **ATP** is made, with no water splitting, oxygen or NADPH.

questions.solution_md: Photosystems and products.

questions.stem_md: Why can the light reaction go on making ATP in far-red light that cannot support oxygen release?

answer.model_answer_md: Far-red light of wavelength beyond 680 nm **excites photosystem I but not photosystem II**. Only **cyclic photophosphorylation** can occur: the electrons circulate through PS I and the cytochrome complex and **ATP is made**. With PS II idle there is **no water splitting and no oxygen**.

questions.solution_md: Only PS I excited; cyclic flow.

marking_scheme.step: Only PS I is excited beyond 680 nm
Cyclic flow makes ATP; no water splitting or oxygen

questions.stem_md: Name the three events that raise the proton concentration in the thylakoid lumen relative to the stroma.

answer.model_answer_md: First, **splitting of water** inside the lumen releases protons. Second, the carrier **plastoquinone** takes protons from the stroma and releases them in the lumen as it passes electrons on. Third, **NADP reductase** uses protons from the stroma to reduce NADP⁺, **lowering the stroma concentration** further.

questions.solution_md: Three events.

questions.stem_md: Explain the chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis in the thylakoid, naming the parts of ATP synthase.

answer.model_answer_md: As electrons flow, **protons accumulate in the lumen**, building a **gradient** across the thylakoid membrane. **ATP synthase** has a transmembrane channel, **CF₀**, and a knob, **CF₁**, on the stroma side. Protons flow back down their gradient through CF₀; the **breakdown of the gradient** releases energy that causes a **conformational change in CF₁**, which makes **ATP** from ADP and phosphate.

questions.solution_md: Gradient; CF0 and CF1; ATP formation.

marking_scheme.step: Gradient breakdown changes CF₁; ATP made

questions.stem_md: Describe how the two photosystems work together in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and state the final products.

answer.model_answer_md: In **PS II** (P680) light excites electrons, which pass **downhill** through plastoquinone, the cytochrome b₆f complex and plastocyanin to **PS I**. Water splitting replaces the lost electrons. In **PS I** (P700) light excites the electrons again; they pass through ferredoxin to **NADP reductase**, which makes **NADPH**. The products are **ATP, NADPH and oxygen**.

questions.solution_md: PS II to PS I to NADP.

marking_scheme.step: PS II excitation and downhill transfer

questions.stem_md: Describe the light reaction of photosynthesis. Include the photosystems, non-cyclic electron flow, the source of oxygen, how ATP is made by chemiosmosis, and how cyclic flow differs.

answer.model_answer_md:
Pigments are organised in **photosystems I and II**, each with an antenna of pigment molecules and a chlorophyll a **reaction centre**: **P700** in PS I and **P680** in PS II.

**Non-cyclic flow (Z scheme).** Light excites PS II; electrons pass downhill through plastoquinone, cytochrome b₆f and plastocyanin to PS I, excited again, and then through ferredoxin to **NADP reductase**, which makes **NADPH**. Electrons lost by PS II are replaced by **splitting of water**, the source of the **oxygen**.

**Chemiosmosis.** Water splitting, proton transport by plastoquinone and use of stromal protons by NADP reductase build a **proton gradient** in the lumen. Protons flow out through **CF₀** of **ATP synthase**; CF₁ changes shape and makes **ATP**.

**Cyclic flow** uses **PS I only**; electrons return to PS I, making **ATP alone**.

questions.solution_md: Photosystems, Z scheme, oxygen, chemiosmosis, cyclic.

The CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle** with **RuBisCO**, and the 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll to regenerate PEP.

In **C₄ plants** the first product is the 4-carbon **oxaloacetic acid**, there is **Kranz anatomy** with the Calvin cycle in bundle sheath cells, **photorespiration is absent**, the **temperature optimum is higher** and productivity is greater.

questions.stem_md: What is photorespiration? Explain why it is wasteful and why C₄ plants do not show it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Photorespiration** is the pathway that begins when **RuBisCO binds O₂** in place of CO₂ at high O₂ and low CO₂, so RuBP gives **PGA and phosphoglycolate**. It is **wasteful** because **no sugar, ATP or NADPH** is made and **CO₂ is released**. **C₄ plants** avoid it because they **concentrate CO₂ at RuBisCO** in the bundle sheath cells, so O₂ cannot compete.

questions.solution_md: Definition; waste; absence in C4.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Calvin cycle in three stages. State the enzyme of the first stage, the ATP and NADPH used per CO₂, and the totals for making one glucose.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **Calvin cycle** takes place in the **stroma**.

**Carboxylation:** CO₂ combines with **RuBP** (5C), catalysed by **RuBisCO**, to give two molecules of **PGA** (3C), the first stable product.

**Reduction:** PGA is phosphorylated and reduced to **triose phosphate (G3P)**, using **2 ATP and 2 NADPH** for each CO₂ fixed.

**Regeneration:** RuBP is regenerated so the cycle continues; this needs **1 ATP** per CO₂.

So each CO₂ costs **3 ATP and 2 NADPH**. One glucose needs **6 turns**, that is **18 ATP and 12 NADPH**. In three turns, 3 RuBP and 3 CO₂ give 6 PGA and then 6 G3P; five of these regenerate 3 RuBP and one is the net gain.

questions.solution_md: Three stages with enzyme and totals.

marking_scheme.step: Totals: 3 and 2 per CO₂; 18 and 12 per glucose

questions.stem_md: A student says that C₄ plants have no Calvin cycle. Evaluate this claim by describing the C₄ pathway and the leaf anatomy that supports it, and give two advantages of C₄ plants.

answer.model_answer_md:
**The claim is wrong.** C₄ plants fix CO₂ twice and the Calvin cycle still operates.

**Anatomy.** Kranz anatomy: large **bundle sheath cells** with thick, gas-tight walls and no intercellular spaces surround the vascular bundles.

**Pathway.** In the **mesophyll cells** **PEP carboxylase** fixes CO₂ onto **PEP** (3C) to form **oxaloacetic acid** (4C), converted to malic or aspartic acid. These move to the **bundle sheath cells** and release **CO₂** and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle**, with **RuBisCO** present only here, and the 3-carbon molecule returns to regenerate PEP.

**Advantages.** C₄ plants have **no photorespiration**, a **higher temperature optimum** and respond to high light, giving **greater productivity**.

questions.solution_md: Claim rejected; anatomy; pathway; advantages.

marking_scheme.step: PEP carboxylase, OAA, transfer, release of CO₂

questions.stem_md: State Blackman’s law of limiting factors and illustrate it with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Blackman’s law** states that if a process is affected by more than one factor, its **rate is determined by the factor nearest its minimal value**. questions.stem_md: Describe the effects of light, temperature and water on the rate of photosynthesis.

answer.model_answer_md: **Light:** the rate rises with intensity and **saturates at about 10 percent of full sunlight**. **Temperature:** the **dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature sensitive**, and **C₄ plants have a higher optimum** than C₃ plants. **Water:** water stress **closes the stomata**, lowering the supply of CO₂, and wilting reduces the leaf surface.

questions.stem_md: State Blackman’s law of limiting factors and describe how light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water affect the rate of photosynthesis, with the difference between C₃ and C₄ plants.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Blackman’s law (1905):** if a process is affected by more than one factor, its **rate is determined by the factor nearest its minimal value**.

**Light:** the rate rises with intensity and levels off, since other factors then limit; **saturation occurs at about 10 percent of full sunlight**.

**Carbon dioxide:** the major limiting factor, since air has only **0.03 to 0.04 percent**. At high light **C₄ plants saturate at about 360 µL per L**, while **C₃ plants respond up to about 450 µL per L**, which is why greenhouse tomato and bell pepper give more with CO₂ enrichment.

**Temperature:** dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature controlled; **C₄ plants have a higher optimum** than C₃ plants.

**Water:** stress closes stomata, reducing CO₂, and wilting reduces leaf area.

questions.solution_md: Law and four factors, C3/C4.

A grower records the rate of photosynthesis of tomato plants (arbitrary units) in a greenhouse at 25 °C.

| Trial | Light (percent of full sunlight) | CO₂ (µL per L) | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 450 | 22.5 |
| 2 | 10 | 300 | 30 |
| 3 | 10 | 450 | 45 |
| 4 | 20 | 450 | 45 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Light

**(b)** 15

**(c)** (i) By **Blackman’s law** the rate is set by the factor **nearest its minimum**. In trial 4 the light is more than enough, so **CO₂ is limiting again**; with the CO₂ unchanged at 450 µL per L, **more light cannot raise the rate**.

**OR** (ii) Since **CO₂ is limiting** in trial 4, the grower can **enrich the greenhouse air with CO₂**. C₃ plants such as tomato respond to CO₂ up to about 450 µL per L and beyond, so the rate **would rise** until another factor, such as temperature or light, becomes limiting.

**(b)** $45 - 30 = 15$ units.

(ii) Enrich with CO2.
